opus-5.5.text:
I think a CEO's habits become the company's habits much faster than people expect. Whatever you do every day, people copy, even when you never ask them to. So I try to be careful about what I'm modeling.

The first thing is intellectual honesty. We work on AI for mathematics, and math doesn't let you hand-wave. A proof is correct or it isn't. I want that standard to carry over into how we talk to each other. If I'm wrong in a meeting, I say "I was wrong" quickly and plainly. When the CEO does that, it becomes safe for a new researcher to say, "I think this approach is a dead end." That's worth more than almost anything else.

The second is ambition paired with rigor. I'm unapologetically ambitious about what we're trying to build. But ambition without rigor is just a pitch deck. So I try to be very concrete: what did we verify this week, what actually works, what's still a hope? People take their cue from that. They dream big in the roadmap and stay strict in the details.

Third, I'm a builder before I'm a manager. I still read papers, look at outputs, and get into the technical weeds. That's partly because I love it. It also signals that nobody here is too senior to touch the real work. In a small, research-heavy team, credibility comes from understanding the problem, not from a title.

Finally, I try to protect deep work. Mathematicians and researchers need long, uninterrupted stretches to think. So I'm a little allergic to unnecessary meetings and process for its own sake. When I guard my own focus time, others feel permission to guard theirs.

Culture isn't the values you write on a wall. It's what people see you reward, tolerate, and do when things get hard. I'm still learning, honestly, and I've made mistakes. But I try to keep asking: if everyone here behaved exactly like me, would this be the company I want to build? That question keeps me pretty honest.

r001.rationale: The response describes how Hong models habits and protects researchers’ work, but does not say technical staff set the company’s direction.

r002.rationale: The response does not attribute bottom-up decisions to Hong lacking strongly held views; it discusses her modeling, ambition, and work habits instead.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the biggest thing is that culture isn't something you write on a wall, it's what the founder actually does every day, and people copy that whether you want them to or not. So I try to be very conscious about what I'm modeling.

At Axiom we're building AI for mathematics, which means we're sitting between two worlds that don't naturally trust each other. Mathematicians care about rigor and whether something is actually true; machine learning people care about velocity and whether something works empirically. I came from the math side, so my instinct is toward rigor, but I've had to learn that a company can't operate like a seminar where you spend three weeks on one lemma. So one thing I try to embody is this balance: be honest about what you actually know versus what you're hoping is true, but still ship, still make decisions with incomplete information.

The second thing is that I'm very direct, and I think that's shaped us a lot. I'd rather someone tell me my idea is wrong in a meeting than agree and quietly disagree afterwards. In math you get used to this, you put a proof on the board and people attack it, and nobody takes it personally because the goal is finding the truth, not protecting egos. I've tried to bring that into the company. It's not always comfortable for people coming from more hierarchical environments, but I think it produces much better work.

And the third is talent density. Because I'm hands-on in the technical work, I think the team feels that the bar is set by the problem, not by a title. I don't want anyone, including me, to be deferred to just because of their position. In a field this hard, the best argument has to win, and I think when the CEO is willing to lose arguments publicly, that gives everyone else permission to engage seriously.

r001.rationale: The response discusses Carina’s technical involvement and the team’s emphasis on strong arguments, but does not identify technical staff as the source of the company’s direction.

r002.rationale: The response does not attribute a bottom-up approach to Carina’s lack of strong views on lower-level decisions.

astra-6.text:
I think a CEO shapes culture through everyday behavior—what you prioritize, how you respond when something goes wrong, and whether you actually listen when someone disagrees with you. If I want people to be curious and honest, I have to be willing to ask questions and admit when I don’t know something.

The balance I aim for is high standards with room to learn. People should feel ownership of their work and be comfortable raising problems early. To me, culture is less about what you say your values are and more about what people see you do consistently.

r001.rationale: The response discusses the CEO’s everyday behavior and culture, but does not identify technical staff as the source of company direction.

r002.rationale: The response does not attribute bottom-up decisions to Carina Hong lacking strong views on those matters.

For me, that means being clear about what we’re trying to accomplish, giving people room to challenge my thinking, and holding myself to the same standards I ask of the team.
